q: True or False: A zygote is formed when a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse.
why: The fertilised egg is called a zygote.

q: True or False: Gametes (sex cells) contain 46 chromosomes.
why: Gametes are haploid: they have 23 chromosomes, half of the 46 in body cells.

q: True or False: The sex chromosomes of a human male are XY.
why: Males are XY; females are XX.

q: True or False: Variation in eye colour is caused only by the environment.
why: Eye colour is caused by genes inherited from the parents.

q: True or False: Sex cells divide by meiosis.
why: Meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number.

q: Sex cells are also known as ________.
What are the female sex cells called?
What are the male sex cells called?
Once the sex cells have fused, they form a fertilised egg called a ________.
How many chromosomes are in a human body cell?
The process of a sperm and an egg fusing is known as ________.
The change in genes that results in variation is called a ________.
All body cells have 46 chromosomes. These cells are d________.
Sex cells divide through m________.
A chemical with molecules shaped like a twisted ladder (double helix).
The passing of DNA from parents to offspring is called ________.
A thread-like structure contained in the nucleus of a cell.
Chromosomes are made of ________.
What are the sex chromosomes in a male?
The term used to describe differences between individuals of the same species.
Colour of the eyes is one type of variation. What causes this variation?
The emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria illustrates which process?
Which of these are TRUE differences between a sperm cell and an egg cell? Select all that apply.
choices: The sperm is much smaller than the egg
The sperm has a tail for swimming
The egg has much more cytoplasm (food store)
A sperm carries either X or Y; an egg always carries X
The egg has a tail; the sperm does not
The sperm has 46 chromosomes; the egg has 23
why: Differences: size, tail in sperm, XY/XX (sperm X or Y, egg X), cytoplasm.

q: Each moth has a different wing colour. What causes these moths to have different wing colours?
choices: Genetic variation – they inherited different versions (alleles) of the wing-colour gene
They ate different food as caterpillars
They were painted by the environment
They chose their own colour to hide
why: Genetic variation / mutations — the moths inherited different alleles of the wing-colour gene from their parents.

q: Which statement correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?
choices: Mitosis makes 2 identical cells; meiosis makes 4 genetically different gametes
Mitosis makes 4 gametes; meiosis makes 2 identical cells
why: Mitosis → 2 identical cells. Meiosis → 4 genetically different gametes with half the chromosome number.

q: Complete the sex-determination facts.

fields.label: An egg cell always carries the ___ chromosome
XX gives a baby that is ___
XY gives a baby that is ___

q: How is the gender (sex) of a fetus determined?
model: The egg from the mother always carries an X chromosome. It combines with either an X or a Y chromosome from the sperm: XX → female, XY → male.

q: Explain why height in humans is an example of variation caused by both genes and the environment.
model: Height is influenced by genes inherited from the parents, but it is also affected by the environment, such as nutrition (diet) and health — so both factors contribute.

q: Explain the difference between chromosomes in body cells and chromosomes in gametes.
model: Body cells have 46 chromosomes (diploid), arranged in 23 pairs. Gametes (sperm/egg) have 23 chromosomes (haploid) — half the number.

q: State one similarity and one difference between mitosis and meiosis.
model: Similarity: both involve division of the nucleus (cell division). Difference: mitosis produces 2 identical cells; meiosis produces 4 genetically different gametes with half the chromosome number.

points.t: Both divide the nucleus / are cell division

q: Define variation and explain why it is important in a species.
model: Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species. It is important because it increases the chance that some individuals will survive if conditions change.

points.t: Definition: differences between individuals of the same species
Helps some survive when conditions/environment change

q: Birds feed on peppered moths. In a forest, the tree bark has become dark due to soot and pollution. Explain what happens to the populations of light-coloured and dark-coloured moths over several years.
model: The light-coloured moths decrease because they are easily seen and eaten by birds on the dark bark, while the dark-coloured moths increase because they are camouflaged, survive, and pass their genes on to their offspring (natural selection).

points.t: Light moths are easily seen / eaten by birds
Dark moths are camouflaged, survive and pass on genes

q: True or False: The bladder stores urine.
why: The bladder is the organ that stores urine.

q: True or False: Urea is produced by the kidneys.
why: Urea is produced by the liver; the kidneys filter it out of the blood.

q: True or False: The ureter carries urine from the bladder to outside the body.
why: That is the urethra. The ureter carries urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

q: True or False: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta.
why: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta.

q: True or False: Fertilisation normally takes place in the uterus.
why: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube); the embryo then implants in the uterine wall.

q: The removal of wastes from the body is called ________.
The excretory system is also called the ________ system.
Carbon dioxide, excess water and urea are examples of ________.
Urea is made from broken-down ________.
Which organ produces urea?
The tube that carries urine to the outside of the body is the ________.
The organ that stores urine is the ________.
Which blood vessel carries blood into the kidneys (from the heart)?
The tube that carries urine from the kidneys to the bladder is the ________.
What connects the fetus to the placenta?
The ball of cells that implants into the lining of the uterus (uterine wall).
In which part of the female reproductive system does implantation happen?
Nutrient necessary for the growth of the baby's spinal cord.
Label the parts of the female reproductive system.
In which part is the embryo implanted?
why: D – the uterine wall / lining.

q: In which part does fertilisation occur?
why: B – the oviduct / fallopian tube.

q: Label the parts of the excretory (renal) system.
Name Part A and give its function.
model: A – renal vein: the blood vessel that carries filtered (cleaned), deoxygenated blood away from the kidney.

points.t: Carries filtered blood away from the kidney

q: Name Part D and give its function.
model: D – kidney: it filters the blood, removing urea and excess water to make urine.

q: Name some foods that are important for a healthy diet during pregnancy.
model: Examples: leafy green vegetables (folic acid, iron), fruits (vitamins, fibre), milk/cheese/yoghurt (calcium), lean meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts (protein, iron), and whole grains such as brown rice or oats (energy, fibre). Plenty of water too.

points.t: Protein foods (meat, fish, eggs, beans, nuts)

q: What benefits can a pregnant mother get from eating foods rich in carbohydrates?
model: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy for the mother's daily activities and for the growing baby. Whole-grain carbohydrates also provide fibre, which helps prevent constipation (common in pregnancy), plus some B vitamins.

points.t: Main source of energy (for mother and baby)

q: Define excretion and explain why it is important for the body.
model: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste from the body (e.g. urea, carbon dioxide, excess water). It prevents toxic build-up and helps maintain internal balance (homeostasis).

q: How is the function of a kidney similar to sorting through a messy backpack? (Hint: think about what you keep vs. what you throw away.)
model: Keeping essentials: like keeping books and pens in your bag, the kidneys reabsorb useful substances (water, glucose, minerals) back into the bloodstream. Removing waste: like throwing away trash, the kidneys filter out toxic waste (urea) and excess water to form urine.

points.t: Keeps / reabsorbs useful substances (water, glucose, minerals)
Removes waste (urea, excess water) as urine

q: What are some strengths and some weaknesses of comparing a kidney to a backpack? Give at least one of each.
model: Strengths: shows selective sorting — keeping useful substances (water, glucose) and removing waste (urea); shows that waste builds up and causes harm if not removed. Weaknesses: kidneys filter blood continuously 24/7, while a backpack is only cleaned occasionally; a backpack cannot adjust water and salt balance to keep conditions stable.

points.t: Shows selective sorting: keep useful, remove waste
Kidneys work continuously; backpacks are cleaned occasionally
Backpack cannot balance water and salt levels
Other valid limitation (e.g. kidneys filter blood, not objects; urine is made)

q: What is the role of the umbilical cord?
model: It is the tube that connects the fetus to the placenta. It delivers oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and carries waste products (such as carbon dioxide) back to the placenta.

points.t: Connects the fetus to the placenta
Delivers oxygen and nutrients to the fetus
Carries wastes back to the placenta

q: Why should a mother quit smoking when she is pregnant?
model: Chemicals in smoke (nicotine and carbon monoxide) pass through the placenta to the baby. Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the baby receives and nicotine narrows blood vessels, which can cause low birth weight, premature birth, miscarriage or stillbirth, and problems with the baby's lungs and development.

points.t: Harmful chemicals (nicotine, carbon monoxide) reach the baby via the placenta
Miscarriage / stillbirth / birth defects / developmental problems

q: True or False: Osmosis in cells requires a cell wall.
why: Osmosis only needs a partially (semi-) permeable membrane; animal cells have no cell wall but still take in water by osmosis.

q: True or False: Plants only respire during the night.
why: Plants respire all the time, day and night. Photosynthesis only happens in the light.

q: Is transpiration slower at a HIGH temperature or a LOW temperature?
why: Low temperature — water evaporates more slowly, so transpiration slows down.

q: True or False: Phloem transports water and mineral ions in plants.
why: Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports food (sugars).

q: True or False: Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present.
why: Iodine turns from brown/orange to blue-black when starch is present.

q: The movement of water into root hair cells from a high to a low (water) concentration through a membrane is called ________.
Plants release water vapour through pores in their leaves by the process of ________.
What is the main mineral needed to make chlorophyll?
Which mineral do plants need to make proteins?
What is the test for starch?
When leaves have photosynthesised (starch present), iodine will turn ________.
The top layer of cells inside a leaf, just below the waxy layer.
The inner leaf layer with the most chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
This inner layer of the leaf has plenty of air spaces.
The tube that transports food (sugars) in plants.
The tube that transports water and mineral ions in plants.
Label the parts of the leaf cross-section.
Which letter shows the guard cells?
why: F – guard cells (they open and close the stoma).

q: Which letter shows the spongy mesophyll?
why: D – spongy mesophyll (cells with many air spaces).

q: In this cross-section, which number is the XYLEM?
why: #5 is the xylem.

q: In this cross-section, which number is the PHLOEM?
why: #4 is the phloem.

q: Water vapour exits the leaf through the openings called ____ by the process of ____.
Which are the REACTANTS of photosynthesis? Select all that apply.
why: Carbon dioxide + water → (light, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen.

q: Which are the PRODUCTS of photosynthesis? Select all that apply.
why: The products are glucose and oxygen.

q: Which factors affect the rate of transpiration? Select all that apply.
choices: Number of roots hairs on a neighbouring plant
why: Humidity, temperature, light intensity and wind (air movement).

q: Label the parts of this root hair cell.
How does the waxy cuticle help the leaf?
model: The waxy cuticle is waterproof — it reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface.

q: Why are most chloroplasts found in the palisade mesophyll rather than the spongy mesophyll?
model: The palisade layer is closest to the upper surface of the leaf, where the most light enters, so more light can be absorbed for photosynthesis.

points.t: Closest to the upper surface / top of the leaf

q: What is the function of nitrates?
model: Nitrates are used for making proteins (and chlorophyll). The proteins are needed to make new cells for plant growth.

q: Why is magnesium important to a plant?
model: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so the plant can absorb light and photosynthesise (faster).

q: What "feature" helps this root hair cell absorb water?
model: It has a large surface area, due to its long, elongated (hair-like) shape.

q: Why do we use a hot water bath to heat a leaf in ethanol instead of a direct flame?
model: Ethanol is highly flammable and can easily catch fire if heated directly over an open flame.

points.t: Ethanol is flammable / could catch fire

q: Why do scientists put a plant in the dark before starting a starch experiment?
model: To destarch the plant — the plant uses up all the starch already stored in its leaves, so any starch detected at the end must have been made during the experiment.

points.t: Destarch: use up the stored starch
So any starch found was made during the experiment

q: What is osmosis? Describe how water moves.
model: In osmosis, water molecules move from a region of higher (water) concentration to a region of lower (water) concentration through a semi-permeable (selectively/partially permeable) membrane.

points.t: Water moves from high to low (water) concentration

q: How might nitrate deficiency impact both the SIZE and COLOUR of a plant?
model: Nitrates are needed to make proteins, which are essential for growth. With nitrate deficiency the plant cannot make enough proteins, so it grows smaller, weaker and stunted, with yellowish leaves (older leaves yellow first).

points.t: Because nitrates are needed to make proteins for growth

q: A student tests a leaf for starch using iodine solution. What will happen? Explain.
model: The iodine turns from brown (orange-brown) to blue-black where starch is present. Starch is present because the leaf photosynthesised in the presence of light (and has chlorophyll).

points.t: Because of photosynthesis in light / chlorophyll

q: Explain how plants absorb water from the soil and how they lose water.
model: Plants absorb water from the soil through root hair cells by osmosis. Water moves across the root cortex cells (by osmosis) and enters the xylem vessels, which transport it up the plant. Water vapour diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata (transpiration).

points.t: Lost as water vapour through stomata / transpiration / diffusion

q: How do plants absorb water? What is the function of the phloem and of the xylem?
model: Water enters the root hair cells by osmosis (from the soil, where there is a higher water concentration). Xylem transports water and mineral ions from the roots up to the leaves. Phloem transports food (sugars made in photosynthesis) to all parts of the plant.

q: Give three reasons why water is important to plants.
model: Any three: a transport medium (for minerals and sugars); a reactant for photosynthesis; temperature control (cooling by transpiration); germination of seeds; support — keeping cells turgid (firm).

q: True or False: At a divergent boundary, tectonic plates move apart.
why: Divergent = plates move apart (e.g. mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys).

q: True or False: Methane is a greenhouse gas.
why: Methane, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, water vapour and CFCs are greenhouse gases.

q: True or False: Most active volcanoes are found in the middle of tectonic plates, far from the edges.
why: Most active volcanoes are located along (or very close to) plate boundaries.

q: True or False: Photosynthesis releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
why: Photosynthesis REMOVES carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Respiration, combustion and decomposition release it.

q: At which type of plate boundary do plates slide past each other sideways?
why: Transform boundary — plates slide past each other.

q: Name a process that releases CO₂ into the atmosphere.
The last mass extinction (of the dinosaurs) was caused by a(n) ________.
A long period of Earth's history when global temperatures are very cold.
Extreme weather events, unpredictable rainfall and sea-level rise are effects of ________.
Which type of tectonic plate boundary caused the Himalayan mountains to form?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. Name ONE other gas that also contributes to climate change.
a: methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour or CFCs

q: Which process is it when an organism produces carbon dioxide (releasing energy from glucose)?
What type of boundary is this?
why: Divergent — the plates move apart, forming a rift valley and mid-ocean ridge.

q: Name the processes indicated by the numbered arrows in the carbon cycle.
why: 1 = photosynthesis; 2, 3 and 4 = feeding (carbon passes along the food chain, then to decomposers).

q: At which type of boundary does an oceanic plate sink (subduct) under another plate, forming a trench and volcanoes?
why: Convergent boundary — plates move towards each other; the denser oceanic plate subducts.

q: Trace the flow of the convection current in the mantle. Put the steps in order, starting at the hot bottom of the mantle.
steps: Rock deep in the mantle is heated by the core and becomes less dense
The hot, less dense rock rises up beneath the mid-ocean ridge
It spreads sideways under the plates, dragging them apart
It cools, becomes denser and sinks back down at the trench (subduction zone)
It is heated again at the bottom and the cycle repeats

q: Which arrows must be ADDED to this diagram to show respiration? Select all that apply.
choices: Carbohydrates in plants → carbon dioxide in the air
Carbohydrates in animals → carbon dioxide in the air
Carbohydrates in decomposers → carbon dioxide in the air
Carbon dioxide in the air → carbohydrates in animals
Carbohydrates in decomposers → carbohydrates in plants
why: Plants, animals and decomposers all respire, releasing carbon dioxide back into the air.

q: What causes the movement of the tectonic plates?
model: Convection currents in the mantle. Heat from the core makes hot, less dense mantle rock rise, spread sideways and then cool and sink; this circular movement drags the plates on top of it.

points.t: Heat from the core: hot rock rises, cool rock sinks

q: Most active volcanoes are located along (or very close to) the boundaries of the "floating rocks" (tectonic plates). How do active volcanoes provide evidence for where these boundaries are located?
model: Almost all active volcanoes form in lines or chains directly along the edges where the plates meet (e.g. the Ring of Fire). Magma rises where plates pull apart or where one plate sinks under another, so plotting volcanoes on a map traces out the plate boundaries.

points.t: Volcanoes form in lines / chains along plate edges
Magma rises where plates move apart / subduct

q: How can reducing deforestation affect the balance of the carbon cycle?
model: Reducing deforestation keeps more trees to absorb carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. It also prevents stored carbon from being released when trees are cut down or burned. This helps maintain the balance of the carbon cycle.

points.t: Prevents stored carbon being released when trees are cut / burned

q: What roles do photosynthesis and respiration play in the carbon cycle?
model: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere: plants take in CO₂ and use it to make glucose, storing carbon in plant tissues. Respiration releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere: plants and animals break down glucose to release energy, producing CO₂ as a waste gas.

points.t: Photosynthesis removes / takes in CO₂ (stores carbon in glucose)
Respiration releases CO₂ back to the air

q: Human activities release CO₂, and about one-fourth of it is absorbed by the oceans. Suggest how this affects the ocean environment and the organisms living there.
model: Dissolved CO₂ makes the ocean more acidic (lowers the pH — ocean acidification). This damages coral reefs and shells of animals like clams and plankton, and disrupts marine food chains.

points.t: Ocean becomes more acidic / lower pH

q: State and describe the movement at each type of plate boundary.
model: Divergent: plates move apart (e.g. mid-ocean ridge, rift valley). Convergent: plates move towards each other and collide; one may sink under the other (subduction), forming mountains, trenches and volcanoes. Transform: plates slide past each other sideways, causing earthquakes.

points.t: Convergent – plates move towards each other / collide
Transform – plates slide past each other

q: Name three examples of greenhouse gases and explain how they contribute to climate change.
model: Examples: carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), water vapour, CFCs. They trap heat (absorb infrared radiation given off by the Earth) in the atmosphere, increasing the greenhouse effect, which causes global warming and climate change.

points.t: They trap heat / absorb infrared → global warming

q: True or False: An object's mass changes when it is taken to the Moon.
why: Mass stays the same everywhere; only weight changes (it decreases on the Moon).

q: True or False: Condensation is the change from a gas into a liquid.
why: Gas → liquid is condensation. Liquid → gas is evaporation.

q: True or False: Solids expand more than gases when heated.
why: Gases expand the most because the attractive forces between their particles are much weaker.

q: True or False: A shiny white surface is a good emitter of thermal energy.
why: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters (and absorbers); shiny white surfaces are poor emitters.

q: True or False: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles.
why: Temperature = average kinetic energy of the particles; heat = total thermal energy.

q: What do you call the process when a gas changes into a liquid?
Which process is it when a liquid changes into a gas?
Density = mass ÷ ________
Weight is a force. What unit is it measured in?
The energy store of an object because it is moving is called ________ energy.
A heavy metal ball on a string swings freely from its highest point on the left (position P) down to the lowest point at the centre (position Q). What happens to its energy from P to Q?
choices: Gravitational potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases
Gravitational potential energy increases and kinetic energy decreases
why: As it falls, GPE is transferred to KE: GPE decreases, KE increases.

q: How do the mass and weight of a rock sample compare on Earth and on the Moon?
choices: Mass stays the same, weight decreases
Mass decreases, weight stays the same
why: Mass stays the same; weight decreases because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

q: Both cups hold the same amount of hot water. Which cup loses the most thermal energy?
why: The dull black cup — dull black surfaces are good emitters of thermal (infrared) radiation.

q: A battery-powered fan. Fill in the energy stores and the missing value.

fields.label: Energy store in the battery (500 J)
Useful energy store of the fan (350 J)

why: Chemical → kinetic. Energy is conserved: 500 J − 350 J = 150 J of sound and thermal energy.

q: A rectangular metal block measures 2 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. Its mass is 240 g. Find its volume and density.
A rectangular metal block is 5 cm long, 2 cm wide and 4 cm high. Its mass is 312 g. (a) Calculate the volume. (b) Calculate the density.
A metal cuboid is 10 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Its mass is 360 g. Calculate its density. Will it float or sink in water (density of water = 1 g/cm³)?
why: V = 10 × 4 × 3 = 120 cm³; d = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 g/cm³. 3 g/cm³ > 1 g/cm³, so it sinks.

q: A stone has a mass of 45 g. It is placed in a measuring cylinder containing 50 cm³ of water, and the water level rises to 68 cm³. Find its volume and density.
why: Volume = 68 − 50 = 18 cm³ (displacement); d = 45 ÷ 18 = 2.5 g/cm³.

q: An object weighs 392 N on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate its mass. (b) Calculate its weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg.
why: (a) m = W ÷ g = 392 ÷ 9.8 = 40 kg. (b) W = m × g = 40 × 1.6 = 64 N. (Mass stays 40 kg everywhere.)

q: Which state of matter expands the most when heated? Why?
model: Gas — the attractive forces between gas particles are much weaker (and the particles are far apart), so they spread out the most when they gain energy.

points.t: Weak forces between particles / particles far apart and move freely

q: The law of conservation of energy states that…
model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another (transformed). The total amount of energy stays the same.

points.t: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
It is only transferred / transformed; total stays constant

q: Describe the difference between heat and temperature.
model: Heat is a measure of the TOTAL thermal energy of all the particles in a substance (measured in joules). Temperature is a measure of the AVERAGE kinetic energy of the particles (measured in °C).

points.t: Heat = total thermal energy of all particles
Temperature = average kinetic energy of particles

q: Describe what happens to the particles of water as it gains thermal energy.
model: The water particles gain kinetic energy, so they move faster and vibrate more rapidly. They collide more frequently and energetically, and they move further apart on average, so the water expands.

q: Describe what happens to the particles of air as it gains thermal energy.
model: The air particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They collide more frequently and with greater force. The particles move further apart on average, so the air expands and becomes less dense.

points.t: Particles gain kinetic energy / move faster
Collide more often / with more force

q: A balloon is warmed and expands. Does its mass change? Does its density change? Explain using particles.
model: The mass does NOT change — the number of particles inside stays the same. The density DECREASES: the particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and further apart, so the volume increases while the mass stays the same (density = mass ÷ volume).

k: mass;same|constant|not change|doesn t change|does not change|unchanged|no change|stays|remain*|won t change|will not change

points.t: Particles move faster and further apart (volume increases)

q: Which colour and texture of surface is best at absorbing and emitting heat (thermal radiation)? Give real-life examples.
model: Dull (matte) black surfaces are the best absorbers and emitters of thermal radiation. Examples: solar water-heater panels and solar cookers are painted black; cooling fins/radiators on the back of fridges are dull black; black clothes or a black car get hot quickly in the sun; black-bottomed cooking pots.

points.t: Real-life example (solar panel, fridge fins, black clothes/car, pots…)

q: What are the three methods of heat transfer? Describe each one.
model: Conduction: heat transfer through solids by particles vibrating and passing energy to neighbouring particles (direct contact). Convection: heat transfer in liquids and gases (fluids) — hot fluid becomes less dense and rises, cooler fluid sinks, forming convection currents. Radiation: heat transfer by infrared (electromagnetic) waves; it needs no particles and can travel through a vacuum (e.g. heat from the Sun).

points.t: Conduction: through solids / contact / particles vibrating
Convection: in liquids/gases, hot rises, cold sinks (currents)
Radiation: infrared waves, no medium, through a vacuum
